source.title: Toward epidemic thresholds on temporal networks: a review and open questions

accepted.question_text: In temporal-network epidemic models that compute the epidemic threshold from a repeated sequence of adjacency-matrix snapshots A_1, ..., A_T, one often imposes a periodic boundary condition A(T+t) = A_t so that the observed snapshot sequence repeats indefinitely. This repetition can create time-respecting transmission paths that did not exist in the original finite temporal network. Does imposing that periodic boundary condition change the epidemic threshold that is estimated for the original temporal contact network, and if so, how?
accepted.context_brief: Periodic boundary conditions in snapshot models

evidence.quote: However, the approach of Valdano et al. assumes a period boundary condition, A(T+t) ≡ At, where the temporal network snapshots are repeated over time.
The authors note that this may result in time-respecting paths that are not present in the original temporal network, but whether this affects the estimated epidemic threshold is an open question.

accepted.question_text: Temporal contact networks can exhibit coordinated bursts of contacts, such as many individuals temporarily gathering at the same place and time. How do such coordinated bursts affect disease spread and the epidemic threshold on temporal networks?

evidence.quote: In real-world social interactions, it is possible to observe coordinated bursts of contacts.
For example, wildlife may gather at a common water source during a draught, temporarily placing them in close contact. To date, the effects of this phenomenon remain unexplored.

accepted.question_text: Temporal contact patterns may be periodic because of seasonal or other recurring changes in behavior and social interaction. What effect do such periodic contact patterns have on disease spreading and epidemic thresholds in temporal networks?

evidence.quote: Contacts may also exhibit periodic patterns, e.g., due to seasonal changes in behavior and social interaction (Enright and Kao, 2018).

The effect this has on disease spreading has not been explicitly examined in temporal networks, though most temporal network models appear to be capable of extension by simply repeating the time period.

accepted.question_text: Human and other contact networks are often not closed, isolated populations, but are connected across multiple population scales. When temporal contact networks at different scales all change over time, what epidemic and network dynamics emerge from coupling those scales together?

evidence.quote: In nearly all cases, static and temporal contact network models are composed of closed and isolated populations, but in our globally connected world human contact networks commonly have have far-reaching connections.
This may be addressed using a combination of contact network models at different population scales. What dynamics emerge when network changes occur over time at these different scales?

accepted.question_text: When one uses a closed temporal-network model for analytic or computational tractability even though the real population interacts with individuals outside the modeled network, can those external interactions be incorporated statistically in a way that still yields useful epidemic-threshold calculations?

evidence.quote: And, when we require closed models for analytic or computational tractability, can we account statistically for assumed interactions with individuals external to the network?

accepted.question_text: Instead of treating the epidemic threshold as a single critical value, can one formulate it in terms of the probability that an epidemic occurs under a specified set of conditions, such as when transmission and infection parameters are known or can be estimated with reasonable error? More broadly, can epidemic-threshold theory be reframed as a function of epidemic likelihood so that intervention costs and benefits can be evaluated more finely?

evidence.quote: A related problem of interest is to estimate the probability of an epidemic given a particular set of conditions.

The probability of epidemic is not typically estimated in conjunction with the epidemic threshold. Perhaps this could be accomplished by framing the epidemic threshold as a function of the likelihood of epidemic rather than as a singular value.

accepted.question_text: Most epidemic-threshold work on temporal networks assumes that the network is deterministic and fully observed, but many practical settings require uncertainty quantification, prediction of future interactions, and inference of latent community structure. How can results on epidemic thresholds for temporal networks be connected to statistical network models and community-detection methods so that threshold analysis remains usable when the network is only partially known or must be modeled probabilistically?
accepted.context_brief: Statistical network models and community detection

evidence.quote: Most of the existing literature on epidemic thresholds considers the network to be deterministic and fully observed. This approach does not allow for uncertainty quantification or future predictions of interactions.
Connecting the existing results on epidemic thresholds to statistical network models and community detection techniques can greatly broaden the applicability of these results.

accepted.question_text: Small-scale local structures in a temporal contact network, such as unusually dense subgraphs, anomalous cliques, or chain-like patterns, can strongly alter how infection propagates. How can techniques for detecting such local structures be connected to epidemic-threshold analysis, and how exactly do those local structures affect disease dynamics on temporal networks?

evidence.quote: Local structures, i.e., interaction patterns localized to a small part of the network, can play a significant role in the transmission of a diseases through the network.
Connecting these detection techniques to epidemic thresholds and understanding the impact of local structures on disease dynamics is an important open question.

accepted.question_text: Network monitoring can mean either monitoring propagation on a fixed network or monitoring a network that itself changes over time. What are the precise connections between these network-surveillance problems, disease transmission, and epidemic thresholds in temporal networks?

evidence.quote: Both problems have important connections with disease transmission and epidemic thresholds, and studying these connections is still an open question.

accepted.question_text: Epidemic-threshold theory for temporal networks is usually developed under the unrealistic assumption that the full sequence of contact networks is observed. In practical risk assessment, one may only have partial samples or coarse observations of the evolving network. How can epidemic-threshold methods be applied under incomplete observation, with quantified uncertainty from sampling, and what kinds of data are sufficient for reliable prediction in different epidemiological settings?
accepted.context_brief: Applying threshold theory with incomplete data

evidence.quote: While significant advances have been made in the theory of estimating epidemic thresholds on temporal networks, there has been comparatively little progress in understanding how to apply this theory. One key application is that of risk assessment in case of real-world infectious diseases and outbreaks. To date, this has largely been an unexplored area of research.
In most of the current literature on epidemic thresholds, the underlying contact network is assumed to be fully known and observed.
Understanding what kind of data is needed in which epidemiological context is an important direction of future research.
